expectations.text: States that a written agreement or reminder is not enforcement
expectations.evidence: All three rely on someone remembering. That's rung 0 on the poka-yoke scale (training), and training decays

expectations.text: Recommends a pre-commit hook to run the formatter automatically
expectations.evidence: Pre-commit hook running the formatter and a fast type check on changed files

expectations.text: Notes that pre-commit is bypassable with --no-verify and must be backed by a CI check
expectations.evidence: Pre-commit hook... yes (`--no-verify`)... CI required check... **no**, if branch protection is on

expectations.text: Recommends a type check as a required CI check
expectations.evidence: CI required check running the same formatter (`--check` mode, not 'fix and pass') and full type check

expectations.text: Recommends baselining or ratcheting rather than enforcing across the whole repo at once
expectations.evidence: Baseline first, then ratchet... enforce formatting/types on changed files only, or snapshot current violations as a baseline and fail CI only on *new* ones

expectations.text: Notes that branch protection is what makes a CI check actually required
expectations.evidence: this is the one that actually can't be bypassed, but only if it's wired into branch protection as a required status check. A CI job that merely runs and reports isn't enforcement; a red X that blocks merge is.

expectations.text: Recommends the failure message tell the developer how to fix it
expectations.evidence: Make the CI failure teach, not just fail — the message should say exactly what command to run (`npm run format`, `mypy path/to/file.py`)

expectations.text: Does not primarily recommend rewriting CONTRIBUTING.md, more reminders, or more discipline
expectations.evidence: Two of the three prose-based things you did (CONTRIBUTING.md, standup mentions) can stay as *context* for why the rule exists — that's fine, it's just not the enforcement mechanism
